objective: By the end of this lesson you can brief and fly VOR, LOC and RNAV (GPS) LNAV or LP approaches to an MDA, set your real minimums for category, NOTAMs and inoperative equipment, and decide at the VDP or MAP whether to land or go missed.
why: Non-precision approaches have no electronic glidepath, so the pilot builds the descent and guards the MDA alone. Unstable, low and late descents on these approaches are a classic path to controlled flight into terrain.

warmup: On an ILS the glideslope tells you when to descend and where the bottom is. On a VOR or LNAV approach there is no glideslope. What will you use instead to know how fast to descend, how low you may go, and when it is too late to land?

key_terms.def: Lowest altitude in feet MSL you may descend to on final, or while circling, when there is no electronic glideslope.
Altitude on an approach with vertical guidance where you must start the missed approach if you can't see the required references.
Start of the final segment of a non-precision approach. Shown as a Maltese cross in the profile view.
A fix that lets you descend to a lower minimum altitude after you pass an obstacle.
A point (V symbol) on a straight-in final from which a normal descent from the MDA to the touchdown point can start.
Advisory descent angle from the FAF or stepdown fix to the threshold. Helps you fly a steady descent. Gives no obstacle protection below the MDA.
The point where you must start the missed approach if you can't continue. On a non-precision approach it is a fix, a NAVAID or a time from the FAF.
RNAV (GPS) line of minima with lateral guidance only, flown to an MDA. GPS or WAAS may be used.
WAAS line of minima with lateral guidance only, but with localizer-like sensitivity. Flown to an MDA.
The GPS receiver checking the integrity of its own position. Needs 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding.
Marks a route or sector where you may not fly the procedure turn unless ATC clears you to.
How high the straight-in MDA or DA is above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE).

body.p: FAA approach charts use one standard layout, called the Pilot Briefing Information format. It is in a logical order so you can brief the chart from top to bottom [[29:149|IPH 4-9]].

head: Part of the chart
What you find there
rows: The NAVAID and its frequency, the final approach course, runway information, notes (such as altimeter source or radar required) and communication frequencies in the order you will use them [[23:35|IFH 1-16]]
The approach seen from above: routes from the en route structure to the IAF, the procedure turn, obstacle elevations and the MSA [[23:35|IFH 1-16]]
The approach seen from the side: altitudes, distances, FAF, stepdown fixes, VDA and missed approach icons. Not drawn to scale [[23:40|IFH 1-21]]
MDA or DA and visibility for each aircraft approach category, straight-in and circling [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]
Runways and lighting, and on some charts a time and speed table from the FAF to the MAP [[23:46|IFH 1-27]]

body.p: **The title tells you the equipment.** It names the system that gives final approach guidance and the runway, like VOR RWY 13. A letter instead of a runway, like VOR-A, means circling only. A slash means you need both systems (VOR/DME RWY 31). The word "or" means either one will do (VOR or GPS RWY 15) [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a)]]. The FAA is removing the slash and /DME from titles as procedures are amended, so also read the notes, plan view and equipment (PBN) box [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a) NOTE]]. Notes such as ADF REQUIRED or RADAR REQUIRED tell you about other equipment you need, including for the missed approach [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(b)]].

**Altitude symbols.** In the profile, an underlined altitude is a minimum, an overlined altitude is a maximum, and one with both lines is mandatory. An altitude with no line is only recommended. If ATC puts a charted altitude in your clearance, it becomes mandatory [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b]].

callout.text: The MSA is for emergencies. It gives 1,000 ft of obstacle clearance, normally within 25 NM, but it does not promise navigation signal coverage [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5c]].

check.q: A chart is titled VOR/DME RWY 32. What equipment do you need for the final approach?
check.a: Both a VOR receiver and DME. A slash means more than one type of equipment must be used [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a)]].

body.p: An approach has up to four segments: initial, intermediate, final and missed approach. Feeder routes bring you from the en route structure to the IAF [[29:182|IPH 4-42]].

head: Segment
From and to
Job
rows: En route fix to the IAF
Transition. Not an approach segment. 1,000 ft obstacle clearance (2,000 ft in mountains) [[29:182|IPH 4-42]]
Line you up and let you descend: DME arc, course reversal or terminal route [[29:189|IPH 4-49]]
Position you for final. Normally within 30° of the final course [[29:189|IPH 4-49]]
FAF (or final approach point) to the MAP
Descent to the MDA. With no FAF, it starts where you are established inbound after the procedure turn [[29:190|IPH 4-50]]
MAP to a fix where an initial or en route segment begins

body.p: The required obstacle clearance shrinks as you go: 1,000 ft in the initial segment, 500 ft in the intermediate and 250 ft on final in the FAA drawing [[29:190|IPH Figure 4-28]]. That is why you must not descend early.

**Procedure turns.** A procedure turn or hold-in-lieu-of-PT is required when it is charted, unless ATC clears you straight-in. It is not allowed when the route says NoPT, when you get a radar vector to final, or on a timed approach from a holding fix [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a]]. The barbed arrow shows the side to turn on. Where you start the turn and what type you fly are your choice, within the charted distance, unless the chart shows a procedural track that must be flown exactly [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a1]]. Stay within the charted distance, normally 10 NM, and at or below 200 KIAS [[33:427|AIM 5-4-9a3]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.175(j): on a radar vector to final, a timed approach from a holding fix, or a NoPT route, no pilot may make a procedure turn unless ATC clears it. 91.175(i): on a vector or unpublished route, keep your last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i) and (j)]].

body.p: Want to fly a procedure turn that isn't required, maybe to lose altitude? Get an amended clearance first. Unsure whether ATC wants a straight-in? Ask right away [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a NOTE]]. If you are cleared to an IAF that has a course reversal, you must fly it unless cleared straight-in [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h4]].

When a PT fix altitude is published, don't descend to the PT completion altitude until you are over or abeam the PT fix and outbound [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a2]]. In a hold-in-lieu-of-PT, fly the charted direction and don't exceed the charted leg length or time [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a]].

check.q: You are cleared for the approach on a route marked NoPT and you are 1,000 ft high. May you fly the procedure turn to lose altitude?
check.a: Only if ATC clears you to. A NoPT route prohibits the procedure turn unless cleared [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]]. Ask for it, or ask for a hold or vectors [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a NOTE]].

chunks.title: MDA vs DA, stepdown fixes, VDA and VDP

body.p: The MDA is the lowest altitude, in feet MSL, you may descend to on final or while circling when no electronic glideslope is provided [[29:159|IPH 4-19]]. A DA is where you must go missed on an approach with vertical guidance if you don't have the visual references [[29:160|IPH 4-20]].

head: MDA
DA
rows: LNAV, LP and circling lines [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]]; VOR, NDB, LOC and other nonprecision approaches [[29:190|IPH 4-50]]
Descend to the MDA, then level off and fly to the VDP or MAP
Follow the glidepath down to the DA
At the MAP: a fix, a NAVAID or a time from the FAF [[29:190|IPH 4-50]]
On reaching the DA on the glidepath [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]
Never below the MDA unless 14 CFR 91.175(c) is met [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]]
Obstacle clearance allows a momentary dip below DA as you start the missed [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]]

body.p: **Stepdown fixes** let you go lower after passing an obstacle. There is usually only one between the FAF and the MAP [[23:40|IFH 1-21]]. Stepdown altitudes on final apply when you fly to an MDA line. They do not apply to LPV or LNAV/VNAV DA lines. Outside the final segment you must honor them on every approach [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]]. If you can't identify the stepdown fix, its minimum altitude becomes your MDA; circling minimums apply if they are higher and you must circle [[23:40|IFH 1-21]]. Many charts publish a second set of minimums for pilots who can't identify the fix [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].

**VDP.** The V symbol marks the point from which a stabilized visual descent from the MDA to the touchdown point can begin. Don't descend below the MDA before reaching the VDP. It is identified by DME or RNAV along-track distance; if you can't identify it, fly as if there were none [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. VDPs apply only to LP and LNAV minima [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m7(b)]]. Your GPS will not show it as a waypoint, so use along-track distance [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(12)]].

**VDA.** Most non-precision approaches publish a VDA and threshold crossing height. It is advisory only. It does not guarantee obstacle protection below the MDA and it does not change any non-precision rule [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]]. If the chart says Visual Segment- Obstacles instead, following the angle below the MDA may put you into obstacles [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k1]].

callout.text: On RNAV charts, a gray shaded area from the MDA to the runway in the profile means the visual segment is clear of obstacles on a 34:1 slope. No gray area means it is not clear [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Either way, below the MDA you must see and avoid obstacles yourself [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

check.q: The VDP is 1.3 NM from the runway. You reach the MDA at 2.5 NM and already see the runway. Do you start down now?
check.a: No. Hold the MDA until the VDP; you should not descend below the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

chunks.title: RNAV (GPS) approaches: LNAV, LP and the lines with vertical guidance

body.p: An RNAV (GPS) chart has up to four lines of minima. An ATC clearance for the procedure lets you use any minimums your aircraft is certified for. A WAAS airplane may use LPV or LP; a GPS-only airplane may not [[33:415|AIM 5-4-5m]].

head: Line
Type
Flown to
Equipment
rows: WAAS, with an AFM statement that it supports LPV. Sensitivity like an ILS [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]]
WAAS approved for LP in the flight manual. Lateral sensitivity grows near the runway, like a localizer [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]]

body.p: **LP vs LNAV.** Both are lateral only and both use an MDA. LP is published only where terrain or obstacles prevent vertical guidance, and only if it gives lower minima than LNAV. LP is not a fail-down mode for LPV. Some older WAAS boxes can fly LPV but not LP [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]]. LNAV and GPS approaches use a 0.3 NM lateral integrity limit; LPV uses 40 meters [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d1]].

Lincoln RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 has LNAV and circling minima only [[29:200|IPH 4-60]]. The FAF is OPIZU, at or above 3,000 ft. After OPIZU you may descend to 2,200 ft, but no lower until you pass the stepdown fix 3 NM from RW14. After that fix you may descend to the LNAV MDA of 1,600 ft, 401 ft above the 1,199 ft TDZE, with 1 mile visibility for Categories A and B. The VDA is 3.03° with a 48 ft TCH, and the VDP is 1.1 NM from RW14 [[29:208|IPH Figure 4-39]].

A straight-in RNAV (GPS) final without vertical guidance is aligned within 15° of the runway, should be no longer than 10 NM, and usually has a stepdown fix when longer than 6 NM. It gives at least 250 ft of obstacle clearance [[29:200|IPH 4-60]] [[29:201|IPH 4-61]].

**Overlays.** An older approach with "or GPS" in the title may be flown with GPS. LOC, LDA and SDF approaches are not authorized as GPS overlays [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17b5(a)]]. Fly any GPS approach only from a current database, retrieved by name. Building it from manually entered waypoints is not permitted [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(3)]].

callout.text: Lateral only = MDA (LNAV, LP). Vertical guidance = DA (LPV, LNAV/VNAV) [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]]. Advisory vertical guidance on an LNAV or LP approach does not make it a DA approach; the baro altimeter stays primary [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]].

check.q: Your WAAS receiver shows a glidepath on an LP approach. Is the minimum a DA now?
check.a: No. LP is an MDA. Any WAAS vertical guidance on LP is advisory, and the barometric altimeter remains your primary altitude reference [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]].

body.p: **VOR approaches** are among the most used non-precision approaches. The VOR may be on or off the airport, with or without a FAF. All need working VOR equipment and can have MDAs as low as 250 ft above the runway [[29:206|IPH 4-66]]. If DME is in the title, you need working DME to fly it from the FAF [[29:209|IPH 4-69]].

**Localizer approaches.** A localizer is always aligned within 3° of the runway and gives at least 250 ft of obstacle clearance on final [[29:216|IPH 4-76]]. Its course is 700 ft wide at the threshold, full scale left to full scale right [[33:78|AIM 1-1-9b2]]. If the glideslope fails, the ILS becomes a localizer approach [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]]. On a back course a standard VOR indicator senses in reverse, and any glideslope signal must be ignored; an HSI set to the front course removes reverse sensing [[29:216|IPH 4-76]].

Tallulah LOC RWY 36: localizer I-TVR on 109.7, FAF at the NDB at 2,000 ft, 6 NM to the MAP. At 90 knots that takes 4:00. The Category A MDA is 500 ft, 414 ft above touchdown [[29:227|IPH Figure 4-58]]. When the MAP is a time, start your clock at the FAF and figure groundspeed from your approach speed and the wind [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

head: Select, tune and identify
What to check
rows: The only positive ID is the Morse code or the recorded voice ID with the word VOR [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3c]]
Three letters preceded by I, e.g. I-DIA [[33:79|AIM 1-1-9b4]]
No warning flag, so monitor the ID the whole time [[33:68|AIM 1-1-2]]
No ID or a TEST code means maintenance: unreliable. Never fly a procedure that is NOTAMed out of service, even if the ID is present [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]

callout.text: Between 108.0 and 112.0 MHz, VORs use even tenths and localizers use odd tenths [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. Localizers run 108.10 to 111.95 MHz [[33:78|AIM 1-1-9b1]]. A frequency like 108.2 can't be a localizer: re-check the chart.

check.q: You tune the localizer, the needle centers, but you hear no identifier. Can you fly the approach?
check.a: No. Removing the ID warns that the facility is off the air for maintenance and may be unreliable even if signals are received [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]].

chunks.title: GPS annunciations, RAIM and level of service

body.p: RAIM is your receiver checking its own position integrity. It needs 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding. Receivers with fault detection and exclusion (FDE) need 6, or 5 plus baro-aiding. Enter the altimeter setting so baro-aiding works [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17a3(a)]].

head: When
What happens
What you do
rows: 30 NM from the airport, approach loaded
Receiver gives an arm annunciation. Armed, CDI and RAIM go from ±5 NM to ±1 NM terminal sensitivity [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(3)]]
Arm it if it doesn't arm by itself
Approach mode goes active. Full-scale CDI shrinks smoothly from ±1 NM to ±0.3 NM at the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]]
Be established on final before this, and confirm approach active before the FAWP [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(6)]]
No approach mode, or RAIM alert, before the FAWP
GPS no longer gives the required integrity
Don't descend. Fly to the MAWP via the FAWP, go missed, tell ATC [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]]
Climb and fly the missed approach [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(8)]]
Shows the best level of service: LPV, LNAV/VNAV, LP or LNAV available [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]
Fly to the minimums that match the annunciation

body.p: Receivers don't fail down once the approach is active. If only the vertical flag appears, you may use LNAV minima if your rules allow changing approach type. If the lateral limit is exceeded on an LP approach, you must go missed [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2 NOTE]].

**The ramp-down trap.** As the scale tightens, a needle that isn't centered moves out, so it can look like you are flying away from the course. Cross-track error helps. Don't accept vectors that join final within 2 NM of the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

**Before the flight.** Get a RAIM prediction from a manufacturer tool, the FAA SAPT website or flight service [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(2)]]. If RAIM won't be there, plan another approach, route or destination, or delay [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(5)]]. Non-WAAS GPS under IFR needs another approved way to navigate, and you must monitor it when RAIM is lost [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(a)(2)]].

callout.text: Cleared for an RNAV (GPS) approach, fly it from an IAWP or feeder fix; joining at an intermediate fix does not assure terrain clearance [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(2)]]. On the missed, the receiver won't sequence past the MAWP until you tell it to, and turns should not begin before the MAWP [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]].

check.q: 1 NM before the FAWP your receiver still has not changed from armed to approach active. What do you do?
check.a: Don't descend to the MDA. Fly to the MAWP and go missed; the RAIM and CDI will not ramp down [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]].

chunks.title: Your real minimums: category, NOTAMs and inoperative components

body.p: The authorized MDA is the highest of three: the one on the procedure, the one set for you as PIC, and the one for the equipment you have and use [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

**Category.** Your approach category is based on VREF, or 1.3 VSO at maximum landing weight if no VREF is given: A under 91 knots, B 91 to 120, C 121 to 140, D 141 to 165 [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. If you fly faster than your category's top speed, use the higher category's minimums. A Category A airplane flying a straight-in at 130 knots uses Category C [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

**Inoperative components.** Published minimums assume every component and visual aid for the approach works. When one is out, higher minimums may apply [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. If the glideslope fails, the ILS becomes a non-precision localizer approach and you use the LOC minimums. If the localizer fails, the ILS approach is not authorized [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]].

callout.text: Older handbook pages send you to an Inoperative Components table in the front of the TPP, with fixed raises such as ¼ mile for an ILS with its approach lights out [[23:313|IFH 10-22]] [[23:46|IFH 1-27]]. Those values are older samples, so don't memorize them; check the front of the current TPP. For the approach you will fly, read its minimums, its notes and the NOTAMs to see how an outage changes your MDA and visibility.

body.p: Obstacles in the visual segment can also raise the published visibility, remove the VDP, or make the procedure not authorized at night. The chart notes tell you [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

**Altimeter source.** Minimums assume the local altimeter setting unless the chart says otherwise. A note may let you use another source and raise the MDAs. If no authorized setting is available, the approach is not authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]]. Tallulah's note: if the local setting isn't received, use Monroe Regional and increase all MDAs 140 ft [[29:227|IPH Figure 4-58]].

bullets: Check NOTAMs for the airport, NAVAIDs and GPS before every approach [[29:142|IPH 4-2]] [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(a)(6)]].
When a stepdown fix can't be identified, a second set of minimums may be published for you [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].
RVR not reported? Convert: 2,400 RVR = ½ mile, 4,000 = ¾ mile, 5,000 = 1 mile [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)(2)]].

callout.text: Highest MDA wins: procedure, PIC, equipment [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]]. Then check category, altimeter source, NOTAMs and chart notes.

check.q: The glideslope on the ILS you planned is NOTAMed out of service. What minimums do you use?
check.a: The localizer (LOC) minimums. With the glideslope out, the ILS becomes a non-precision localizer approach flown to an MDA [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

chunks.title: Stabilized approach, energy and descent math

body.p: A stabilized approach keeps a constant approach speed, descent rate, vertical path and configuration in the final stages. It is strongly recommended for propeller airplanes. Keep configuration changes at low altitude to the ones you can handle easily [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Cross the FAF at the right airspeed, altitude and configuration [[29:159|IPH 4-19]].

**Energy.** Your total energy is the sum of your altitude and your airspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Pitch plus power controls your energy state [[24:92|AFH 4-6]]. Poor energy management contributes to loss of control, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Trying to stretch a low approach with pitch alone bleeds airspeed and leads to a high sink rate or a stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

callout.text: A descent rate over about 1,000 fpm is unacceptable below 1,000 ft AGL, in the instrument or the visual part of the approach [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

head: Tool
How
Example
rows: Look up angle and groundspeed in the TPP rate of descent table [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k3]]
3.0° at 90 knots = 478 fpm; at 120 knots = 637 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]
Height above TDZE = NM from threshold × 300
Where will I reach the MDA?

body.p: Fly that rate on the VSI and you have a steady path. A constant-rate descent has safety advantages over several level-offs at stepdown fixes, and keeps you stabilized from the FAF to landing [[29:165|IPH 4-25]]. Plan to reach the MDA where you can still land in the touchdown zone: at the VDP, or at a point you calculate [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

check.q: The FAF is 2,000 ft, the TDZE is 86 ft and the FAF to MAP time is 4:00. What descent rate does the IPH method give?

chunks.title: At the MDA: see it, or go missed

body.p: You may go below the MDA only when all three are true: you are continuously in position to land on the intended runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers; the flight visibility is at least what the approach requires; and at least one required visual reference is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)-(3)]].

bullets: Approach light system. With the approach lights alone you may not go below 100 ft above TDZE unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].
Threshold, threshold markings or threshold lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(ii)-(iv)]].
Runway end identifier lights or the visual glideslope indicator [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(v)-(vi)]].
Touchdown zone, its markings or its lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(vii)-(viii)]].
The runway, runway markings or runway lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(ix)-(x)]].

body.p: **Go missed immediately** if the requirements are not met while below the MDA, or on arriving at the MAP, or at any time after that until touchdown [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. You may not land if the flight visibility is below the published visibility [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]]. Only you can judge flight visibility; if it is too low, go missed whatever the report says [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

There is no obstacle protection from the MDA to touchdown. You must see and avoid obstacles [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]]. Delay at the MAP puts you at risk of hitting obstacles in the visual segment [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Watch for shallow fog: you may see down but not ahead well enough to flare [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

**Missed approach.** Obstacle protection assumes you start the missed at or above the MDA at the MAP and climb at least 200 ft per NM. If you go missed early, fly to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning, unless ATC says otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. Tell ATC and then request what you want next [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21a]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21f]].

head: Go-around step
How (AFH)
rows: Full or maximum allowable power, smoothly, at once. Carburetor heat off [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Climb attitude without letting airspeed decay. Expect forward pressure and right rudder. Rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Retract flaps partially, in small steps. Flaps before gear; gear up after a positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

check.q: At the MDA you see only the approach lights, without red bars. How low may you descend with that reference?
check.a: To 100 ft above the TDZE. Below that you need the red terminating or side row bars, or another reference [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: a non-precision approach

bullets: 1. **Plan early.** Get weather, field conditions and NOTAMs, figure approach speed and power, set up the radios, and review the procedure [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]. Brief it out loud even when alone; the brief doubles as a checklist [[29:182|IPH 4-42]] [[29:175|IPH 4-35]].

2. **Set up the navigation.** Tune, identify and set the course for each NAVAID. Put the primary NAVAID on the radio that keeps working on battery power [[29:175|IPH 4-35]]. For GPS, load the whole approach by name and check that the waypoints match the chart and are in a logical order [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]].

3. **Talk.** Tell ATC at once if you can't fly the approach they gave you [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4b]]. At a non-towered airport, after "change to advisory frequency approved," announce the approach, your position and when inbound over the FAF [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4d]].
4. **Follow the clearance.** On vectors, keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. Unsure? Ask right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].
5. **Before the FAF.** Slow to approach speed, configure, run the checklist. Hold altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots and no more than ¾-scale CDI (ACS IR.VI.A.S9).

6. **At the FAF.** Start the clock if the MAP is timed [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. Set power and pitch for the planned descent rate [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. On GPS, confirm approach active [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(6)]].

7. **On final.** No more than ¾-scale CDI, airspeed ±10 knots, and at the MDA stay within +100/-0 ft to the VDP or MAP (ACS IR.VI.A.S12). Don't go below any stepdown altitude before its fix [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].
8. **Decide.** References and in position at the VDP: normal descent to land. Nothing at the MAP: missed approach at once [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c) and (e)]].
9. **Use everything.** The MFD moving map shows your position against the course [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. SRM means using all resources, including automation and ATC [[30:56|RMH 8-3]].

head: ACS standard
Tolerance
rows: Altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots, no more than ¾-scale CDI (ACS IR.VI.A.S9)
No more than ¾-scale CDI, airspeed ±10 knots, MDA +100/-0 ft to the VDP or MAP (ACS IR.VI.A.S12)

callout.text: Using an altitude preselector? Set the MDA exactly. If it only moves in 100 ft steps, round up: set 700 for an MDA of 660 [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

body.p: If a navigation or approach instrument fails in flight, tell ATC as soon as practical: who you are, what failed, how it affects you, and what help you want [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. On the checkride you will fly at least two different non-precision approaches: one with a course reversal, one from an IAF without autopilot or vectors, and one on backup or partial-panel instruments (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: On final you are at the MDA, 70 ft high. Are you within the ACS standard?
check.a: Yes. The standard is MDA +100/-0 ft to the VDP or MAP. Going even 1 ft below the MDA without the required references is not allowed (ACS IR.VI.A.S12).

chunks.title: Risk: deviations, frequencies, automation, configuration, weather and the MDA

head: Hazard
Why it bites
How you manage it
rows: Terrain clearance is assured only if you follow the charted altitudes and paths [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a5]]. Flying GPS point to point is not the published procedure [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(8)]]
Fly the full approach as cleared, honor every stepdown, and fly to the MAP before turning [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]
A NAVAID under maintenance can give a believable but bad signal [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. Some GPS installations stop GPS navigation when any ILS frequency is tuned [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m3(a) NOTE]]
Read the frequency from the chart, identify every NAVAID, and check NOTAMs [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3c]]
A wrong MDA in the preselector can take you below it. A wrong GPS entry can drop the approach mode [[29:176|IPH 4-36]] [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(10)]]
Verify every setting out loud. Know your receiver well; use its simulator mode on the ground [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(a)(4)]]
Big speed and configuration changes late degrade awareness [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. A go-around with flaps or gear left down can leave no climb performance [[24:103|AFH 4-17]]
Configure before the FAF. Go-around: power, attitude, then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Over- or under-banking onto final can force high descent rates later [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(4)]]
Plan a rate from the table or timing, and go missed if you can't stabilize
Reported visibility can differ from what you see; shallow fog can hide the runway at the flare [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]
Only flight visibility counts for going lower and landing [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. Keep an alternate and fuel ready
No obstacle protection below the MDA, VDA or not [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]]
Don't let landing expectancy or pride delay the go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]

callout.text: Before every non-precision approach, say: my MDA, my visibility, my VDP, my MAP, my missed. If any one is unclear, ask or don't start.

check.q: Why is following the VDA below the MDA, without seeing the runway environment, dangerous?
check.a: The VDA is advisory and gives no obstacle protection below the MDA. You must see and avoid obstacles in the visual segment [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

bullets: Descending below a stepdown altitude before passing the fix [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].
Leaving the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].
Following the VDA below the MDA when the chart warns of visual segment obstacles [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k1]].
Not checking that the GPS went from armed to approach active before the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]].
Accepting a final intercept within 2 NM of the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].
Flying a procedure turn on a NoPT route or after a vector to final [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]].
Forgetting to raise minimums for category, inoperative components or a remote altimeter setting [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].
Turning early on a missed approach started before the MAP [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].
Go-around errors: indecision, delay, abrupt or not enough power, wrong pitch, wrong configuration [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Diving to the MDA at high descent rates near the ground [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

check.q: Which common error leads straight into terrain on a stepdown approach?
check.a: Descending to the next lower altitude before passing the stepdown fix. Stepdown altitudes protect you from obstacles before the fix [[23:40|IFH 1-21]] [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].

scenario.title: Lincoln RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 in lowering mist
scenario.setup: You fly a Category A single-engine airplane with an IFR-approved, non-WAAS GPS into Lincoln, Nebraska, planning 90 knots on final. ATIS: wind 140 at 8, visibility 1½ miles in mist, ceiling 500 overcast and lowering. Approach control: "Cross SILOY at or above 3,100, cleared RNAV (GPS) Runway 14 approach." You plan to use the autopilot to the FAF. Use Figure 4-39.

questions.q: Do you fly the hold-in-lieu-of-PT at OWABY? What altitudes may you descend to on the way to OPIZU?
questions.a: No. The SILOY leg is NoPT, so no course reversal unless ATC clears it [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]]. Cross SILOY at or above 3,100, hold 3,100 to OWABY, then descend to 3,000 for OPIZU [[29:208|IPH Figure 4-39]].

questions.q: Which minimums apply and what is your MDA?
questions.a: With non-WAAS GPS you use LNAV: MDA 1,600 ft, 1 mile, 401 ft above touchdown for Category A [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(e)]] [[29:208|IPH Figure 4-39]]. If you flew faster than 90 knots you would need Category B minimums, which here are the same [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

questions.q: Crossing OPIZU at 90 knots groundspeed, what descent do you set up, and how low may you go before the stepdown fix?
questions.a: The VDA is 3.03°; the table gives 478 fpm for 3.0° at 90 knots, so about 480 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. Do not go below 2,200 ft until passing the stepdown fix 3 NM from RW14 [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]]. Confirm approach active before OPIZU [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(6)]].

questions.q: What do you set in the autopilot altitude preselector, and when do you set the missed approach altitude?
questions.a: Set the MDA, 1,600, and double check it so the airplane can't descend below it. After you level at the MDA, set the missed approach altitude of 3,100 [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

questions.q: The mist thickens. You reach the RW14 waypoint at 1,600 ft with no runway references. What now?
questions.a: Go missed immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. Power, attitude, then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Sequence the GPS past the MAWP, climb to 3,100 direct ALAWI and hold, and tell ATC [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21a]].

questions.q: In the hold, ATIS now reports visibility ½ mile. Do you try again?
questions.a: Under Part 91 the report alone doesn't stop another try, but you may go below the MDA or land only with flight visibility of at least the 1 mile the LNAV line needs [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2) and (d)]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. With ½ mile reported and the weather going down, another approach is unlikely to work. The safer plan is to request clearance to your alternate [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21f]].

skills.do: Fly the non-precision approaches the evaluator picks: at least two different ones, one with a course reversal, one from an IAF without autopilot or vectors, and one on backup or partial-panel instruments (ACS Appendix 3).
skills.practice: Practice a VOR, a LOC and an LNAV approach, flying at least one full procedure from an IAF with a course reversal [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a]].

skills.do: Talk to ATC as the approach goes on, with correct phraseology, and make the CTAF calls at non-towered airports.
skills.practice: Say your FAF-inbound call out loud on every practice approach: approach type, position, intentions [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4d]].

skills.do: Select, tune, identify and confirm every NAVAID or the GPS approach you will use.
skills.practice: Before every approach, identify each NAVAID by Morse code [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3c]] and check the GPS waypoints against the chart [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]].

skills.do: Comply with every clearance from ATC or the evaluator.
skills.practice: Read back altitudes and approach clearances, and hold the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]].

skills.do: Recognize inaccurate or failed instruments or navigation and take the right action.
skills.practice: Have your instructor fail a NAVAID, a display or GPS integrity. Respond as the AIM says [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]] and report it to ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

skills.do: Tell ATC or the evaluator promptly when you can't comply with a clearance.
skills.practice: Practice saying "unable" with a reason and what you need instead [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4b]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

skills.do: Complete the right checklists for descent, approach, landing and missed approach.
skills.practice: Use your approach briefing as a checklist on every approach [[29:182|IPH 4-42]].

skills.do: Set the right configuration and airspeed for the weather and conditions.
skills.practice: Be at approach speed and configuration before the FAF, and limit changes after it [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[29:159|IPH 4-19]].

skills.do: Before the final segment, hold altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots, no more than ¾-scale CDI, and track courses accurately (ACS IR.VI.A.S9).
skills.practice: Fly the intermediate segment trimmed and stable, with the course set early so you are established before the GPS ramp-down 2 NM out [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

skills.do: Adjust the MDA and visibility for category, NOTAMs, inoperative equipment and inoperative visual aids.
skills.practice: For each practice approach, write down your MDA and visibility after applying category, altimeter source, NOTAMs and any chart notes about inoperative components [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]] [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]] [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]].

skills.do: Set up a stabilized descent to the appropriate altitude.
skills.practice: Look up the rate of descent for the VDA and your groundspeed before the FAF, then fly it on the VSI [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k3]] [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

skills.do: On final, no more than ¾-scale CDI, airspeed ±10 knots, and MDA +100/-0 ft to the VDP or MAP (ACS IR.VI.A.S12).
skills.practice: Level at the MDA with a planned power setting so you don't sink below it. Use along-track distance to find the VDP [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(12)]].

skills.do: Decide whether the required visual references are there, then land or go missed.
skills.practice: Call out the visual references by their 91.175 names during practice approaches, and go missed at the MAP when you don't have them [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3) and (e)]].

skills.do: Use the MFD and other moving-map displays, if installed, to monitor position and wind drift.
skills.practice: Cross-check the moving map against the CDI on every approach [[23:123|IFH 5-28]].
Plan who does what: you, the autopilot and ATC. Manage workload and use all resources inside and outside the airplane [[30:56|RMH 8-3]].

quiz.q: An approach chart is titled VOR or GPS RWY 15. What does that mean?
options: Both VOR and GPS must be used on the final approach
Either VOR or GPS may be used for the final approach
GPS may be used only for the missed approach
The approach is for circling only
quiz.why: "Or" in the title means either type of equipment may be used for the final approach. A slash would mean both [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a)]].

quiz.q: You are on radar vectors and get an approach clearance. When may you descend to the published altitudes?
options: As soon as you hear the approach clearance, on the heading assigned
When you are within 10 NM of the FAF on the vectored heading
When established on a published segment of the approach
Only after crossing the FAF inbound on the final approach course
quiz.why: Keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published route or approach segment, then published altitudes apply [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a published VDA on a non-precision approach is true?
options: It turns the approach into one with a DA
It lets you skip the stepdown fix altitudes
You must follow it exactly to the runway
It is advisory and gives no obstacle protection below the MDA
quiz.why: The VDA is advisory only. It does not guarantee obstacle protection below the MDA and doesn't change any non-precision rules [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]].

quiz.q: Which describes an LP line of minima?
options: Lateral only, flown to an MDA, needs approved WAAS
A fail-down mode that a WAAS receiver uses when LPV is lost
Available to any IFR-approved GPS receiver, WAAS or not
Flown to a DA with WAAS vertical guidance, like LPV
quiz.why: LP uses WAAS lateral guidance with localizer-like sensitivity and an MDA. It is not a fail-down from LPV, and the receiver must be approved for LP [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]].

quiz.q: A RAIM alert appears after you pass the FAWP. What should you do?
options: Hold at the FAWP until RAIM returns
Continue to the MDA using the VDA
Climb and fly the missed approach
Switch to LNAV/VNAV minimums
quiz.why: If the RAIM annunciation appears after the FAWP, initiate a climb and execute the missed approach; the navigation is advisory only [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(8)]].

quiz.q: Your airplane's 1.3 VSO is 75 knots, but you fly the straight-in at 95 knots. Which category minimums do you use?
options: Category B, since 95 knots falls in its speed range
Category C, since you are flying faster than 1.3 VSO
Category A, since 1.3 VSO is under 91 knots
Category D, since the approach speed is above 90 knots
quiz.why: Flying faster than the top of your category means using the higher category's minimums. 95 knots is in Category B (91 to 120) [[29:148|IPH 4-8]] [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

quiz.q: What is the most descent rate the IPH calls acceptable below 1,000 ft AGL on approach?
options: About 500 fpm at most on any approach
About 1,500 fpm, once you are stabilized
About 2,000 fpm, once you are stabilized
About 1,000 fpm, and no more than that
quiz.why: A descent rate greater than about 1,000 fpm is unacceptable in the final stages of an approach, below 1,000 ft AGL [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3) visual references?
options: The rotating airport beacon
Runway end identifier lights
The visual glideslope indicator
Threshold markings
quiz.why: The list includes REIL, the VGSI and threshold markings, but not the airport beacon [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

quiz.q: The chart's minimums are based on the local altimeter setting and no other source is authorized. The local setting is not available. What does that mean for you?
options: Use the GPS altitude instead
Use the nearest airport's setting and add 140 ft
The approach is not authorized
Add 100 ft to the MDA
quiz.why: When the altimeter setting the approach is based on is not available, the approach is not authorized. Another source may be used only when the chart authorizes it, and then the chart says how much to raise the MDAs [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

quiz.q: When a procedure turn is required, what limits apply?
options: Fly the 45° turn exactly as charted; no other type of turn is allowed
Stay within the charted distance, normally 10 NM, at or below 200 KIAS
Stay within 4 NM of the facility, at the published holding speed
Start descent to the PT completion altitude at the IAF inbound
quiz.why: Complete the PT within the distance in the profile, normally 10 NM, and observe 200 KIAS maximum [[33:427|AIM 5-4-9a3]]. The type of turn is the pilot's choice unless specified [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a1]].

takeaways: Non-precision means lateral guidance only: VOR, LOC, LNAV and LP are flown to an MDA.
Your MDA is the highest of procedure, PIC and equipment, then raised for category, altimeter source and inoperative aids.
Never go below a stepdown altitude before the fix, or below the MDA before the VDP.
Watch the GPS: armed at 30 NM, approach active by the FAWP, RAIM good. If not, don't descend.
Fly a planned, steady descent rate from the table or timing; never over about 1,000 fpm low.
Below the MDA only with the 91.175(c) references and flight visibility; at the MAP without them, go missed at once.
cfi_notes: The IPH (4-26) calls the LNAV/VNAV minimum an MDA. The AIM (5-4-5m1(c) and m6(b)) says LNAV/VNAV is published as a DA. Teach the AIM.
The IPH (4-26) says LP is being phased out. The current AIM (5-4-5m1(d)) still describes when LP is published and how it is flown. Teach the AIM and point out the IPH line.
IFH 1-30 says descent below the MDA is not authorized. The correct rule is 14 CFR 91.175(c): you may descend below the MDA when all three conditions are met.
IFH 1-23 defines approach category by 1.3 VSO only. Current 14 CFR 97.3 uses VREF if specified, otherwise 1.3 VSO at maximum certificated landing weight.

IFH 10-13 lists 'a holding pattern is published in lieu of a procedure turn' among cases when a procedure turn is not authorized. That is confusing: AIM 5-4-9a says the hold-in-lieu-of-PT is required when charted unless cleared straight-in. Teach the AIM.

IFH 1-27, 10-22 and Figure 1-23 (and the AIM 1-1-9j reference) describe an Inoperative Components table in the front of the TPP. Its values are older samples, so don't teach its ½ and ¼ mile raises as rules: check the front of the current TPP, and the chart's own notes and NOTAMs. Teach students to read the minimums, notes and NOTAMs for the procedure they will fly.

Examiners often ask: MDA vs DA, LP vs LNAV, what the VDP means, what to do with a RAIM alert before and after the FAWP, and what a glideslope outage or a remote altimeter setting does to the minimums. Have students brief these from a real chart.
Use the Lincoln and Tallulah charts to drill the descent math until students can set a VSI target before the FAF without hesitation.
gaps: Current FAA guidance on how inoperative components change minimums is not in the sources. The IFH and AIM describe a TPP Inoperative Components table, but only older IFH sample values are in the sources; check the current TPP. The current TPP rate of descent table and legend pages are also missing; only older IFH samples are included.
Exact GPS annunciation words and button sequences vary by receiver; the AIM describes only generic arm, active and level-of-service annunciations. Students need their receiver's manual.
AC 120-108 (continuous descent final approach) is not available; CDFA and stabilized approach content comes from the IPH and AIM.
Airplane-specific approach speeds, power settings, configurations and checklists come from the POH/AFM, which is not in the sources.
NDB approach flying technique (ADF tracking) is covered only briefly in the IPH and is not taught in this lesson.

activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

activities.title: True or false: GPS on the approach
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: With the approach loaded, the receiver arms 30 NM from the airport and the CDI goes to ±1 NM.
cards.why: Yes. Armed, CDI and RAIM change to ±1 NM terminal sensitivity within 30 NM [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(3)]].

cards.s: If a RAIM alert appears before the FAWP, you may still descend to the MDA using the VDA.
cards.why: No. Don't descend. Fly to the MAWP via the FAWP, go missed and contact ATC [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]].

cards.s: During an approach, a WAAS receiver automatically fails down from LPV to LNAV when vertical integrity is lost.
cards.why: No. Receivers don't fail down once the approach is active. With only a vertical flag, you may choose LNAV minima if your rules allow [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2 NOTE]].

cards.s: RAIM needs at least 5 satellites, or 4 satellites plus baro-aiding.
cards.why: Yes. FDE needs 6, or 5 plus baro-aiding [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17a3(a)]].

cards.s: A published VDP shows up in your GPS as a waypoint in the approach sequence.
cards.why: No. A VDP is not in the waypoint sequence; use along-track distance [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(12)]].

cards.s: Starting 2 NM before the FAWP, full-scale CDI shrinks from ±1 NM to ±0.3 NM.
cards.why: Yes. It ramps down smoothly and reaches ±0.3 NM at the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

activities.title: Descent and minimums math
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: FAF altitude 2,000 ft MSL, TDZE 86 ft, FAF to MAP time 4:00. Using the IPH method, what descent rate do you use?
The VDA is 3.0° and your groundspeed is 120 knots. What rate does the TPP descent table give?
items.why: Read the 3.0° row in the 120 knot column: 637 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

items.q: A timed approach has 6 NM from the FAF to the MAP. Your groundspeed is 100 knots. How many seconds from the FAF to the MAP?
items.why: 6 ÷ 100 = 0.06 hr × 3,600 = 216 seconds (3:36). Start the clock at the FAF [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

items.q: TDZE is 1,199 ft. Using 300 ft per NM, what altitude MSL should you be at 2 NM from the threshold on a 3° path?
Tallulah LOC RWY 36, Category A MDA 500 ft. The local altimeter setting isn't available, so you use Monroe's. What is your MDA?
items.why: The chart note says increase all MDAs 140 ft: 500 + 140 = 640 ft [[29:227|IPH Figure 4-58]] [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

activities.title: No runway at the MAP: the go-around
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Decide at the MAP: no required references, go missed
Apply full power smoothly, carburetor heat off
Set a climb attitude without losing airspeed, and rough trim
Retract flaps partially, in small steps
With a positive rate of climb, raise the gear (if retractable)
Fly the published missed approach and tell ATC

activities.title: Fly the Lincoln LNAV approach
activities.intro: You are flying N52TR, a Category A airplane with IFR-approved non-WAAS GPS, inbound to Lincoln, Nebraska for the RNAV (GPS) RWY 14 (Figure 4-39). Weather is 500 overcast, 1½ miles in mist. ATC says: "Cross SILOY at or above 3,100, cleared RNAV (GPS) Runway 14 approach."

steps.s: You cross SILOY at 3,100 and turn toward OWABY on the NoPT leg. You feel a little high and fast.
options: Fly the hold-in-lieu-of-PT at OWABY to lose altitude
Ask ATC to give you the LPV line instead of the LNAV line
Descend now to 2,200 to get ahead of the profile
Continue straight in, and ask ATC first if you want a turn in the hold
steps.why: On a NoPT route you may not fly the course reversal unless ATC clears it [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]] [[33:425|AIM 5-4-9a NOTE]]. 2,200 is allowed only after OPIZU [[29:208|IPH Figure 4-39]], and a GPS-only airplane can't use LPV [[33:415|AIM 5-4-5m]].

steps.s: About 2 NM before OPIZU the receiver goes to approach active. The CDI needle starts to move away from center though your heading hasn't changed.
options: Expect it: the scale tightens to ±0.3 NM; check cross-track error
Go missed at once, because the GPS has clearly failed
Turn hard toward the needle to recenter it as quickly as possible and hold it
Switch the CDI back to terminal sensitivity to stop the needle movement
steps.why: As sensitivity ramps from ±1 to ±0.3 NM, an off-center needle moves out. Cross-track error keeps you oriented [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]]. Overriding the sensitivity cancels the approach mode [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]].

steps.s: You cross OPIZU at 3,000 ft, groundspeed 90 knots. The VDA is 3.03°.
options: Dive at 1,200 fpm straight down to 1,600 to make the stepdown early
Descend at about 480 fpm, not below 2,200 until the stepdown fix
Descend at about 300 fpm to save the engine and stay stable
Hold 3,000 until the stepdown fix, then descend at 1,200 fpm
steps.why: 3.0° at 90 knots is 478 fpm in the descent table [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. Stepdown altitudes apply until you pass the fix [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]], and over about 1,000 fpm low is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

steps.s: Level at 1,600 ft, you pass the VDP 1.1 NM from RW14 and see runway end identifier lights flashing ahead. Flight visibility looks a good mile, and you can make a normal descent to the runway.
options: Stay at 1,600 until you see the runway itself
Go missed: REIL is not a valid reference
Begin a normal descent to land
Descend below 1,600 at 1,500 fpm to land quickly
steps.why: REIL is one of the listed references, flight visibility meets the 1 mile minimum, you are in position for a normal descent [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]], and you have reached the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]] [[29:208|IPH Figure 4-39]].

steps.s: At 300 ft above the ground, fog hides the lights and the runway. You are still before the RW14 waypoint.
options: Keep descending a little longer, since the runway is straight ahead
Level off at 300 ft and wait for the lights to reappear before going on
Go missed now, climb on the final course and turn only after the MAP
Turn toward ALAWI right away to begin the missed approach
steps.why: Below the MDA without the required references you must go missed immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. On an early missed, fly to the MAP before turning [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]; the GPS won't sequence until past the MAWP [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: On the Lincoln RNAV (GPS) RWY 14, between OPIZU and the stepdown fix 3 NM from the runway, what is the lowest altitude you may fly on the LNAV line?
options: 1,600 ft, the lowest altitude shown on the LNAV line
2,200 ft, the minimum until the stepdown fix
3,000 ft, the altitude at which you cross OPIZU
2,000 ft, 200 ft below the minimum until the fix
final_quiz.why: 2,200 ft is the minimum after OPIZU until the stepdown fix; 1,600 is allowed only after it [[29:208|IPH Figure 4-39]] [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].

final_quiz.q: Groundspeed on final is 90 knots and the VDA is 3.0°. About what rate of descent should you set?
options: About 480 fpm, the rate for 90 knots at 3.0°
About 320 fpm, the rate for 60 knots at 3.0°
About 640 fpm, the rate for 120 knots at 3.0°
About 800 fpm, the rate for 150 knots at 3.0°
final_quiz.why: The descent table gives 478 fpm for 3.0° at 90 knots [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. 637 is the 120 knot value.

final_quiz.q: Tallulah LOC RWY 36, Category A. The local altimeter setting isn't received, so you use Monroe Regional's. What is your MDA?
options: 500 ft, the published MDA with no correction
640 ft, the published MDA plus the 140 ft
360 ft, the published MDA less the 140 ft
780 ft, the published MDA plus 140 ft twice
final_quiz.why: The note says use the Monroe setting and increase all MDAs 140 ft: 500 + 140 = 640 [[29:227|IPH Figure 4-58]].

final_quiz.q: On the Tallulah LOC RWY 36 your groundspeed is 120 knots. How long from the FAF to the MAP?
options: 3:00, the time for 6 NM at 120 knots
4:00, the time for 6 NM at 90 knots
2:24, the time shown for 6 NM at 150 knots
6:00, the time for 6 NM at 60 knots
final_quiz.why: The chart's table gives 3:00 for 6 NM at 120 knots (6 ÷ 120 × 60 = 3 minutes) [[29:227|IPH Figure 4-58]] [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

final_quiz.q: The localizer of the ILS you planned is NOTAMed out of service, but the glideslope still works. What can you fly?
options: The ILS, using the glideslope only for descent guidance to the DA
The LOC minimums on the same chart, since the glideslope still works
Nothing on that chart: the ILS is not authorized
The ILS, as long as the approach lights are working normally
final_quiz.why: When the localizer fails, an ILS approach is not authorized. Only a glideslope failure lets you fall back to the localizer approach [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]].

final_quiz.q: Flying an LPV approach, only the vertical flag appears. What may you do?
options: Keep flying to the LPV DA, using only the lateral guidance and the VDA
Descend to the LNAV/VNAV DA instead, using the lateral guidance
Wait for the receiver to fail down to LP minimums automatically
Use the LNAV minima if your operating rules allow the change
final_quiz.why: Receivers don't fail down. With only the vertical flag, you may elect LNAV minima if the rules allow changing approach type [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2 NOTE]].

final_quiz.q: At the MDA the reported visibility is 1 mile, the minimum. You see the runway lights, but you judge flight visibility to be ½ mile. What now?
options: Land; the reported visibility is legal
Descend to 100 ft above TDZE and look again
Continue, because you can see the runway lights
Stay at or above the MDA and go missed at the MAP
final_quiz.why: You need flight visibility at least the published minimum to go below the MDA and to land [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2) and (d)]]. Only the pilot can judge flight visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

final_quiz.q: You decide to go missed 2 NM before the MAP while at the MDA. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Turn at once toward the missed approach holding fix
Fly to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning
Climb straight ahead and turn at 400 ft AGL
Descend to gain speed, then climb
final_quiz.why: On an early missed, fly the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA before any turn, unless ATC says otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

final_quiz.q: ATC clears you direct to an IAF that has a hold-in-lieu-of-PT and says "cleared RNAV Runway 14 approach." Nothing about straight-in. What do you do?
options: Fly straight in; the hold is optional
Fly the hold-in-lieu-of-PT, then the approach
Hold until ATC gives an expect further clearance time
Ask for vectors before accepting the clearance
final_quiz.why: Proceeding to an IAF with a published course reversal, you must fly it unless ATC clears you for a straight-in approach [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h4]].

final_quiz.q: Why should you avoid vectors that join final within 2 NM of the FAWP on a GPS approach?
options: RAIM is not checked inside 2 NM of the final approach waypoint
The visual descent point is inside 2 NM of the waypoint
The CDI scale is changing then, which makes the intercept hard to judge
ATC radar loses you inside 2 NM of the final approach waypoint
final_quiz.why: From 2 NM out the CDI ramps from ±1 to ±0.3 NM, so needle movement can mislead you. Be established before then [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

final_quiz.q: Which frequency could be a localizer?
options: 112.5 MHz, a frequency used by VOR stations
108.2 MHz, a frequency used by VOR stations
110.4 MHz, a frequency used by VOR stations
109.7 MHz, a frequency used by localizers
final_quiz.why: Localizers use odd tenths from 108.10 to 111.95 MHz; even tenths between 108.0 and 112.0 are VORs [[33:78|AIM 1-1-9b1]] [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: On a VOR RWY 22 approach, the stepdown fix on final is a cross radial from a second VOR. Your second nav radio fails, so you can't identify the fix. No separate minimums are published. What is your lowest altitude on final?
options: The published MDA, because the stepdown fix doesn't matter here
The FAF altitude, held all the way to the missed approach point
The stepdown fix's minimum altitude, which becomes your MDA
The MSA, since it guarantees obstacle clearance within 25 NM
final_quiz.why: If a stepdown fix can't be identified, its minimum altitude becomes the MDA for the approach [[23:40|IFH 1-21]]. Where the chart has a second set of minimums for this case, use those [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].

final_quiz.q: Your altitude preselector moves only in 100 ft steps and the MDA is 660 ft. What do you set?
options: 700 ft, the next step above the MDA
650 ft, rounded to the nearest 50 ft
600 ft, the step just below the MDA
800 ft, two steps above the MDA
final_quiz.why: Round up so the airplane can't descend below the MDA: 700 ft, as in the IPH example [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

final_quiz.q: A non-WAAS GPS airplane is cleared for an RNAV (GPS) approach with LPV, LNAV/VNAV and LNAV lines. Without baro-VNAV, which line can it use?
options: LPV, because the clearance lists that line
Any of them, since the clearance covers all three lines
LNAV/VNAV, because any GPS gives the vertical guidance
LNAV, the line a non-WAAS GPS supports
final_quiz.why: The clearance lets you use any minimums your aircraft is certified for. GPS-only equipment supports LNAV; LPV needs WAAS and LNAV/VNAV needs baro-VNAV or WAAS [[33:415|AIM 5-4-5m]] [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1]].
